extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, litigators, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and doctrinal guidance on patent litigation procedure (venue, stays, priority among suits, appeals) and substantive patentability requirements (subject matter, utility, novelty, nonobviousness, disclosure, claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue for inducement or contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: As to the inducer or contributor, venue is appropriate only in the district where he or she acted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inducers or contributors are properly sued only in districts where they took the actionable step(s); venue for direct infringers may be broader under §1400(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular and established place of business (28 U.S.C. §1400(b) second test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'regular and established place of business' element does not require that the place of business be related to the alleged infringing act; it is merely a requirement for a certain level of business presence in the district.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inquiry focuses on whether the defendant does its business through a permanent and continuous presence in the district, not whether the defendant has a fixed physical presence such as an office or store.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the general venue statute (28 U.S.C. §1391) in patent-related declaratory judgment suits
rubrics_metrics.description: When the plaintiff alleges a cause of action that arises under the patent laws, and it is not a patent infringement action against a nonalien defendant, the general venue statute applies; a declaratory judgment action that a patent is invalid, unenforceable, or not infringed invokes the general venue statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A declaratory judgment suit, though the mirror image of an infringement action, is governed by the general venue statute rather than §1400(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity and burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is presumed valid; each claim is presumed valid independent of other claims. The burden on the party challenging validity is to show, by clear and convincing evidence, that the patent is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption is never destroyed; in an infringement suit, if the alleged infringer fails to prove invalidity, the court may conclude only that the patent has not been proven invalid. Courts give deference to prior PTO examination but are not bound by PTO decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to PTO decisions in validity challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Although courts are not bound by the PTO's decision to issue a patent, the PTO is due the deference given a qualified government agency that is presumed to have properly done its job.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A challenger presenting no evidence different from that reviewed by the examiner faces a difficult task; presenting material evidence not considered by the examiner should make the challenger's task less difficult, but the statutory burden of proof is not lessened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's inherent power to stay proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: A court has the power to stay proceedings before it because it is within the court's inherent power to control its docket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stays may be used for many reasons; statutory mandates may require stays under certain circumstances (e.g., 28 U.S.C. §1659 for parallel ITC proceedings). Decisions whether to stay are fact-specific and draw on general stay principles (e.g., Landis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority rule for multiple suits (first-filed rule) when parties are the same
rubrics_metrics.description: If the parties in the suits are the same, the priority rule generally applies so that the first-filed suit proceeds while the second-filed suit is stayed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: where the patent owner sues a manufacturer first and the manufacturer files a mirror declaratory judgment action, the second-filed action is usually stayed. An exception exists if there is no reasonable basis for the plaintiff's choice of forum in the first-filed suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: When priority rule is not decisive (different parties or interests)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the parties in the suits are not the same, which suit should proceed is usually not determined by priority alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider identity/real parties in interest, whether both real parties appear in one action (significant factor), and other peripheral issues to decide which suit should go forward; transfer under 28 U.S.C. §§1404 or 1407 may also be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowing PTO proceedings (reissue/reexamination) to proceed first
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court may be asked to stay a patent infringement suit until a PTO proceeding (reissue or reexamination) involving the same patent is resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical scope of reissue/reexamination influenced prior stay decisions; statutory reexamination is narrower than former expanded reissue. Courts have granted and denied stays pending reexamination—decision depends on case-specific considerations of the utility of the PTO process to resolve issues central to litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prior adjudication holding patent invalid — collateral estoppel (Blonder-Tongue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject to one exception, a patent owner whose patent is held invalid in a final and appealable judgment is collaterally estopped from asserting that patent again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exception is where the patent owner did not have a full and fair opportunity to litigate the issue (procedurally, substantively, or evidentially) in the earlier suit; Blonder-Tongue dramatically restricted mutuality of estoppel in patent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for determining 'full and fair opportunity' to litigate (Blonder-Tongue factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court presented five nonexclusive factors relevant to whether the patent owner had a full and fair opportunity to litigate:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Did the patent owner pick the time and the place to litigate (was the patent owner the plaintiff)? 2) Did the patent owner have ample incentive to litigate? 3) Did the court that held the patent invalid apply the proper standards (specifically, the test regarding nonobviousness)? 4) Did the court that held the patent invalid completely fail to grasp the technical subject matter or the issues? 5) Was the patent owner deprived of crucial evidence? Courts may consider only factors related to whether the patent owner had a full and fair opportunity to litigate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prior adjudication where patent was not held invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: A single victory on the issue of validity does not make a patent invincible; when a patent is not held invalid it means the challenger in that case did not present clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior holding regarding validity is entitled to some weight in later suits, but this weight decreases as the quality and quantity of new evidence presented by a new challenger increase; any challenger must be allowed to present his or her evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Circuit jurisdiction and law application on appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 1982, appeals from final decisions of district courts in cases arising under the patent laws go to the Federal Circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit applies its own law when reviewing patent claims; it applies the substantive law of the relevant regional circuit when reviewing accompanying nonpatent claims (e.g., antitrust); procedural issues unrelated to patent issues are decided under the law of the relevant regional circuit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core conditions of patentability (four statutory conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an invention to be patentable, it must be (1) of patentable subject matter, (2) useful, (3) new, and (4) nonobvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before an inventor can obtain a patent, he or she must also (1) be an original inventor, (2) avoid statutory time bars, (3) adequately disclose the invention, and (4) distinctly claim the invention. Formal PTO requirements also apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter categories (35 U.S.C. §101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are granted only on certain tangible subject matter: processes, machines, manufactures (articles of manufacture), and compositions of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideas, theories, and economic theories are not patentable; product/process claims can coexist in one patent; classification into categories need not be specified when seeking a patent. A product of nature is not patentable unless altered by man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims: limits on patentable processes
rubrics_metrics.description: A process is a way to produce a result; the inventor need not know why it works, but not all processes are patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Processes that require mental participation or the mechanical equivalent of mental participation are generally not patentable; processes requiring emotional reactions as an element are also not patentable. The patent is for the discovered and disclosed process, not for explanation of the scientific theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions: machine, composition of matter, manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine is an assemblage of parts that transmit forces, motion, and energy; a composition of matter is a new substance resulting from combinations; a manufacture is anything man-made that is not a machine or composition of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a machine's process is to be patented, process rules apply; printed matter is not a manufacture unless structure or relation of printing to structure is patentable; examples differentiate patentable vs nonpatentable printed matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility requirement (useful)
rubrics_metrics.description: A product or process is not patentable unless it is useful; at the very least, it must work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It need not work perfectly or be superior to competitors. However, inventions usable only for immoral or illegal purposes, that are not sufficiently safe, or that only produce useless products are not useful (and thus not patentable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (new) — anticipation and inherency
rubrics_metrics.description: A product or process is not new if all the elements of that product or process are present in a single piece of relevant prior art; elements present expressly or inherently will defeat novelty (inherency doctrine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation is a question of fact. Prior art comparison is necessary to determine novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 102(a) prior art — 'known' (public knowledge) standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 102(a): 'the invention was known ... by others in this country ... before the invention thereof by the applicant for patent.' 'Known' has been interpreted to mean publicly known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public knowledge counts only if sufficient to enable one of ordinary skill in the art to reduce the invention to practice. Private or secret knowledge is not within §102(a) (e.g., classified government knowledge typically excluded).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 102(a) prior art — 'used' (public use) standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 102(a): 'the invention was ... used by others in this country ... before the invention thereof by the applicant for patent.' 'Used' has been interpreted to mean publicly accessible use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicly accessible use is the absence of affirmative steps to conceal; use must be of the invention reduced to practice and beyond the experimental stage. Operation in an open field may be public use even if unseen; operation under secrecy likely is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 102(a) prior art — patents and printed publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 102(a) bars patents when the invention was patented or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country before the applicant's invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A published patent or printed publication that adequately describes and enables the invention is part of the prior art; 'printed' is broadly interpreted to include tangible material accessible to the public (photographs, distributed conference papers unless recipients were asked to keep them secret). The date of publication is the date first available to the public; published patents place claims and disclosures into prior art, while unpublished foreign patents may place only claimed material into prior art.
